passage: Saturday night. Today was my birthday. Gopika promised on Monday and again on Thursday that she would come. I put the balloons up myself and kept the good chair for her. She did not come, and no one called. I kept looking at the door while we cut the cake. Everyone else was there, and Nani kept calling me the birthday girl, but my chest felt heavy. I am not going to snap at her, and I will not stop talking to her either. On Monday I will say, "I felt sad when you did not come. What happened?" I want to know first. Sangeeta.

qa.q: How many times did Gopika promise she would come?
qa.a: Gopika promised on Monday and again on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling as she kept looking at the door?
qa.a: She felt hurt and disappointed, and her chest felt heavy even with everyone else at the party.

qa.q: What is Sangeeta's plan for talking with Gopika, and why might it work?
qa.a: She plans to say calmly how she felt and ask what happened. Speaking without snapping gives Gopika a chance to explain and keeps the friendship open. 🙂

qa.q: How might Gopika see Monday's conversation if she had a good reason for missing the party?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that Sangeeta asked rather than accused, and want to explain and apologise.

grounding: A child hurt that her friend missed her birthday plans to tell her calmly what it felt like and ask why.

passage:
Saturday. Kashish kept one chair empty at her birthday table, right next to hers. Shreya had promised, pinky-promised, that she would come. The cake was cut, the games were played, and the chair stayed empty. Kashish smiled for the photos and cried in the bathroom afterwards.
Sunday. She typed an angry message: 'Don't bother talking to me again.' She stared at it, then deleted it.
Monday. At the school gate, Kashish took a breath. 'Shreya, you promised to come on Saturday. I kept a chair for you. It really hurt.' Shreya's face crumpled. 'My Nani fell, and we rushed to the hospital. I didn't have your number with me. I'm so sorry.' Kashish felt the hurt loosen a little. 'Is she okay?' 'She's okay now.'

qa.a: One chair at her birthday table, right next to hers.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when the chair stayed empty?
qa.a: Hurt and let down; she smiled for the photos but cried in the bathroom.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than the angry message?
qa.a: Telling Shreya calmly how it felt and giving her the chance to explain.

qa.q: What was it like for Shreya when Kashish spoke to her?
qa.a: Painful and guilty; her face crumpled because she had a real reason but had still broken her promise.

grounding: Over three days a girl hurt by a friend missing her birthday chooses to tell her calmly and ask why, instead of snapping.

passage: 'Vinita, your friend didn't come to your party and now you won't speak to her? Let your Urmila Aaji tell you what I did once. I was nine. My friend Shobha promised to come for my birthday puja and never came. At school I turned my back on her. When she tried to explain, I said, "Liar," and walked off. I didn't talk to her for a whole month. It felt strong, but inside I was still hurting, every single day. Then my mother asked, "Did you ever tell her how it felt?" I hadn't. So I did. Shobha cried and told me her father had lost his job that week and she had no gift to bring. She had been too ashamed to come. A whole month, wasted.'

qa.q: What did young Urmila call Shobha?
What was young Urmila feeling during the month of silence?
qa.a: Still hurt every day, even though turning her back felt strong.

qa.q: What choice in the story finally helped?
qa.a: Telling Shobha how it felt and hearing her reason, instead of refusing to talk.

qa.q: How had Shobha felt about missing the puja?
qa.a: Ashamed, because her father had lost his job that week and she had no gift to bring.

grounding: A grandmother recalls refusing to speak to a friend who broke a promise, and how telling her calmly revealed the reason.
